19997-amerigo-vespucci:
Amerigo Vespucci gave his name to two continents on slender evidence. This 1907 biography and study weighs the Florentine's letters and voyages. It cites the Baron de Porto Seguro's treatise on Vespucci's character and writings. John Fiske called that Lima-printed work the only intelligent modern treatise on the subject. Varnhagen's research anchors the volume's judgments. Frederick A. Ober wrote this Life and Voyages for the Harper trail.

Whether Vespucci reached the mainland before Columbus's fame settled was long disputed. His published letters may be edited, boastful, or partly forged. Ober sorts the claims for general readers carefully. The naming of America is the book's strange outcome. It is a biography of a reputation as much as a man.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agonistici:
Agonistici, from agon, struggle, was one of the names Donatists gave to followers who went through cities and villages spreading Donatus's doctrine. They first appeared about 317 and claimed to be Christ's champions, fighting with Israel's sword. Laudes Deo, Praises to God, was their war cry. Many barbarous acts and deeds of violence followed.

Whether they called themselves fighters because they fought the Lord's battles, or because fighting those protecting property against their invasions forced their hand, is not clear. Catholics styled them Circumcellions, circum cellas euntes, because they roved among peasants, feeding off those they sought to indoctrinate. The short entry thus sketches a roaming militant wing of Donatism, feared for violence and for living off its rural audience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amerigo-vespu:
Amerigo Vespucci, famous Italian navigator born at Florence on 9 March 1451, died at Seville on 22 February 1512. Third son of the notary Ser Nastagio, he studied physics, geometry, and astronomy, wrote his father a Latin letter on his studies in 1476, and possibly knew Toscanelli. He sailed from Cadiz on 10 May 1497 toward the Fortunate Islands, then west, touching the mainland, Guiana or Brazil, after twenty-seven or thirty-seven days.

On 16 May 1499 he sailed again from Cadiz with Ojeda and Juan de la Cosa. Rounding Cape Verde and crossing the Equator, he sighted Brazil's coast at 4 or 5 degrees south. His Mundus novus, on the third voyage, appeared in 1503 or 1504, and his four-voyage letter in 1507, texts printed with many errors and no critical edition. Attempts to name the New World Columbia failed, and the writer defends Vespucci's honesty against the charges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolici:
Apostolici is the name of four different heretical bodies, and the article sorts them by age and error. In the third century, Encratites in Syria and Asia Minor, borrowing from Tatian or Marcion, practising an excessive asceticism that distorted church teaching. They split into Apostolici, Apotactics, and Hydroparastates, named for customs or tenets. The Apostolici claimed to live the apostles' life, banned marriage and property as evil, took in no married men or owners, then lapsed into Novatianism and finally Manichaeism.

Their names and leaders are unknown. In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries a second Apostolics, or false Apostles, began at Parma in 1260 under Gerard Segarelli, a man of low birth and little learning. He strove to revive apostolic poverty. The entry thus warns readers that one proud name covers several movements, united mainly by claiming the apostles' way of life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arabici:
The Arabici were a small third-century sect, named from Arabia where they flourished and also called Thanatopsychitae, from their error about the soul. Their founder is unknown. They held that the soul perishes with the body, though soul and body both would rise again at judgment day. They were led not by philosophy, the article says, but by reading of 1 Timothy 6:16, which says God only has immortality.

That verse, they argued, gives undying life to God alone and bars its unbroken possession by people. They missed the distinction between immortality as God's own nature and imparted immortality, life given by God to people. Short-lived, the sect returned to the church after about forty years of separation, through Origen's persuasive mediation at a council in 250. The entry is a brief case of exegesis gone wrong and put right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolommeo-a:
Bartolommeo and Vincenzo Carducci, called Carducho in Spain, were Florentine painter brothers of the Spanish School. Bartolommeo, born in 1560, painted little in Florence, then followed Zuccaro to Philip II's court and helped paint the Escorial. With Tibaldi he decorated the Escorial library, Tibaldi the ceiling and Bartolommeo the walls. In 1585 he brought his younger brother, then so young he spoke Castilian as his mother tongue.

Bartolommeo's finest work is the Descent from the Cross in Madrid's San Felipe church; he died in 1608 before finishing the Pardo gallery. Vincenzo, court painter to Philip III in 1609 and later to Philip IV, completed his brother's work with Achilles's history. He lost his reason early in 1638 and died confined, leaving his St Jerome unfinished. He also painted for the Paular Carthusians and defended painting's nobility in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardo-tanu:
Bernardo Tanucci, an Italian statesman, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born poor at Stia in Tuscany in 1698, he died at Naples in 1793 after rising by learning. A law chair at Pisa in 1725 led him to defend, with more heat than scholarship, the Pisan manuscript of the Pandects, the Roman law digest.

King Charles of Naples took him south as councillor, posts superintendent, and finally prime minister. He reformed laws through a commission of jurists, steered Naples through war threats, and governed as regent for the boy Ferdinand. The entry presents a tireless minister who ruled Naples long after his king left for Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-anthony-ba:
Blessed Anthony Baldinucci, a Jesuit missionary of central Italy, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Florence in 1665, he died in 1717 after joining the Jesuits in 1681 and ordination in 1695. His field lay around Frascati and Viterbo, with missions beyond, for the rest of his life.

His preaching methods were startling: great processions from the countryside, penitents in crowns of thorns scourging themselves, and vivid images of hell and judgment. Crowds flocked to missions that shook whole towns. The entry presents a fiery preacher of the baroque age, whose methods modern readers may find hard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-giova:
Blessed Giovanni Dominici, cardinal, statesman, and writer, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Florence in 1356, he died at Buda in 1420. Cured of a speech impediment through St. Catherine of Siena's intercession, he entered the Dominicans at Santa Maria Novella in 1372 after a first refusal, then taught and preached at Venice for twelve years after Paris studies.

He founded strict-observance convents at Venice in 1391 and Fiesole. He served as cardinal and legate to Bohemia under Martin V in 1418. He wrote widely, from vernacular hymns to a four-book guide on governing a household and educating children. His Lucula Noctis defends classical study while opposing paganising humanism. Gregory XVI declared him blessed in 1832.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camillo-almic:
Camillo Almici, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, was born on 2 November 1714 and died on 30 December 1779. He joined the Oratory very young and gave himself to theology, Greek, and Hebrew, Scripture, chronology, history sacred and profane, antiquities, criticism, diplomacy, and liturgy. His contemporaries treated him as an oracle on many subjects, and he ranks among the most celebrated theologians of his order.

His chief works include reflections on a book by Febronius and a critique of Voltaire's works. They also include a dissertation on the martyrs of the Catholic Church and meditations on the life and writings of Father Sarpi. The last critically examines Sarpi's unreliable account of the Council of Trent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-dolci:
Carlo Dolci was a Florentine painter born in May 1616 who died in January 1686. Grandson of a painter, he studied under Vignali and drew notice at eleven with a St. John figure and a head of the Infant Jesus. A careful picture of his mother launched a career of commissions in Florence. He seldom left the city, painting religious works alone through a long life of devotion to art.

Each Passion week, the entry records, he painted a picture of the Saviour, and his brush stayed chiefly with heads of Christ and the Virgin. He is famed for soft, gentle faces, transparent color, fine handling of light and shade, and an ivory-like finish, with a simplicity that seems little short of inspired. Critics such as Hinds called him mawkish, yet the entry names him the last of the Florentine School and the last true master of the Renaissance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-matteuc:
Carlo Matteucci was an Italian physicist born at Forlì in June 1811 who died at Ardenza near Leghorn in July 1868. After a Bologna doctorate in mathematics in 1829, he spent two years at the Paris École Polytechnique. He returned to Forlì in 1831 to experiment in physics. Taking up the Voltaic pile, he opposed Volta's contact theory of electricity and linked decomposition in the cell to work done in the pile's elements.

At Ravenna in 1837 he took charge of the hospital chemical laboratory and a physics professorship, and through Arago and Humboldt he won the Pisa chair of physics. There he pursued work begun from Arago's and Faraday's discoveries with ingenious experiments. His books ranged from animal electro-physiology and a manual of electric telegraphy to lectures on the physical and chemical phenomena of living bodies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carracci:
The Carracci were a Bolognese family of painters, engravers, and etchers whose school shaped Italian art around 1600. Lodovico, born in 1555 and dead in 1619, founded the Eclectic School. Masters Fontana and Tintoretto advised him to quit art, and fellow students mocked him as the ox. Slow and plodding yet determined, he became his nephews' teacher and the family's center.

Agostino, born in 1557, began as a goldsmith and turned to engraving under Cort at Venice. With Lodovico and his brother Annibale he opened the School of the Carracci at Bologna in 1589. Annibale, born in 1560, painted and engraved beside them, while Agostino's natural son Antonio Marziale and Lodovico's pupil Francesco carried the name to Rome. Agostino's Last Communion of St. Jerome at Bologna counts as his masterpiece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catherine-de-:
Catherine de' Medici was born on 13 April 1519 and died on 5 January 1589. Daughter of Lorenzo de' Medici of Urbino and of Madeleine de la Tour d'Auvergne, she was orphaned within weeks of birth. At thirteen she was married to Henry, second son of Francis I of France, in a match arranged to win the friendship of her uncle, Pope Clement VII.

Catherine spent years in the background, childless for a decade and overshadowed at court, until Henry's elder brother died and she became dauphiness. When Henry II took the throne on 31 March 1547 she became Queen of France, though she stayed inconspicuous at first. The article follows her from these quiet beginnings through the religious wars that would define her later career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corpus-juris-:
Alphonse Van Hove's entry defines Corpus Juris Canonici. Corpus denotes a collection of documents, corpus juris a collection of laws, in systematic order. The term never received legal sanction in Roman or canon law, remaining the learned's phraseology, yet it applies in this sense to the Roman Christian emperors' Corpus Juris Civilis.

At present the title commonly covers three collections, with the addition of Gratian's Decree, John XXII's Extravagantes, and further extravagantes. The three are Gregory IX's Decretals, Boniface VIII's Sixth Book of the Decretals, and Clement V's Clementinæ. So understood, the term dates to the sixteenth century, officially sanctioned by Gregory XIII in 1580. About 1150 the Camaldolese monk Gratian, Bologna theology professor, sought to ease practical study's difficulties. Gregory IX's, Boniface VIII's, and Clement's Decretals divide uniformly into five books, books into titles, titles into chapters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cursores-apos:
This entry describes the Cursores Apostolici, the Latin title for the heralds of the papal court. Originating in the twelfth century, they did for the pontifical government what heralds did for civil states. From the sixteenth century they belonged to the Roman Curia in its wider sense. They ranked as members of the pontifical family.

Fixed at nineteen under the major-domo, their duties were varied. They invited guests to consistories and chapel functions, served in the palace, and guarded the conclave doors. They posted papal rescripts on Rome's great basilicas, and summoned attendants to canonizations and cardinals' funerals. As the pope's representatives, their invitation carried the force of a judicial summons. Earlier church messengers resembled them, but the office itself grew from civil heraldry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaetano-capoc: This 1913 reference article on Gaetano Capocci — the Roman composer. William Grattan-Flood notes his famous works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the nineteenth century. A musician among the maestri. His 1860 works are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giulio-bartol: This 1913 reference piece on Bartolocci — the Cistercian Hebraist. Francis X.E. Albert honors his famous Bibliotheca. His pen opened the rabbinic lore. The scholars mine the mighty tomes. The Buxtorf of the Roman schools. His 1687 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-house-of-medi: A 1913 entry on the House of Medici — Florence's rulers. Edmund Gardner unfolds their princely age. They crowned the Renaissance arts. The popes sprang from the mighty house. The patrons of the Florentine glory. Their 1532 duchy is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-primadi: This 1913 reference article on Primadicci — an Italian writer of note. Thomas Plassmann catalogs his works. Little survives about his life. The seventeenth century was his time. The learned press knew his pen. His 1690 works are famed. His 1690 Italian pen is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leonardo-da-v: This 1913 reference piece on Leonardo — the universal genius. Louis Gillet honors his famous brush. His art crowned the Renaissance age. The world bless the mighty name. The fifteenth century knew his fame. His 1519 death is famed. His 1503 Mona Lisa is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-loci-theologi: A 1913 entry on the Loci Theologici — the theological places. Joseph Wilhelm unfolds their scholastic lore. They source the dogmatic proofs. The schools prized the seemly bounds. The theologians cite their kinds. Their 1907 study is famed. Their scholastic form is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-botur: This 1913 reference article on Boturini — the Mexican antiquarian. Adolph Francis Bandelier honors his famous collection. His zeal gathered the Aztec codices. The scholars prized the precious hoard. The eighteenth century knew his name. His 1755 death is famed. His 1755 collection is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-ricci: A 1913 entry on Ricci — the last Jesuit general. Francis Van Ortroy unfolds his tragic rule. He faced the suppressing storm. The order bless the steadfast name. The eighteenth century told his tale. His 1775 death is famed. His 1758 rule is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-pulci: A 1913 entry on Pulci — the Morgante poet. Jeremiah Ford honors his famous epic. His verse mocked the chivalric loves. Florence loved the merry muse. The fifteenth century knew his name. His 1484 death is famed. His 1478 Morgante is famed. His 1478 mock epic is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maria-de-medi: A 1913 entry on Maria de' Medici — the French regent. Georges Goyau unfolds her fateful sway. She ruled the boy-king's realm. France knew the Florentine name. The seventeenth century told her tale. Her 1642 death is famed. Her 1610 regency is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matteo-ricci: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Ricci — the China Jesuit. Joseph Brucker unfolds his famous mission. He wedded the Gospel to Confucius. The East hailed the learned name. The seventeenth century knew his fame. His 1610 death is famed. His 1601 Peking is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mondino-dei-l: Mondino dei Luzzi performed the first public dissections of the Middle Ages at Bologna and wrote the anatomy textbook used for two centuries. This entry covers his career, his Anathomia, and his fame. The restorer of anatomy: his textbook guided surgeons for two hundred years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raffaele-garr: Raffaele Garrucci was the Jesuit archaeologist of Christian art. This entry notes his works, his discoveries, and his erudition. The excavator of the catacombs' art: his fine plates preserved the ancient frescoes of Rome's dark catacombs for scholars and pilgrims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-angela-mer: St. Angela Merici was the foundress of the Ursulines. This entry traces her Brescia, her company, and her cult. The mother of the teaching sisters: her new company crowned Brescia in the 1530s' Lombardy in the city of the plain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-catherine-: St. Catherine de' Ricci was the Dominican mystic. This entry traces her Prato, her ecstasies, and her cult. The saint of the Tuscan convent: her holy ecstasies crowned Prato in the 1540s' convent in the city of Tuscany in the hills.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thaumaci: Thaumaci was the titular see of Thessaly. This brief entry traces its ruins and its bishops. A vanished diocese of Greece: its ancient ruins crowned Thessaly in the books of the geographers in the library of the very old scholars.
doe-osti-17056535-24-hour-results-of-the: Dosimeter labs raced the clock in 2026, and this report gives the 24-hour results of the nuclear accident dosimetry intercomparison. The pages rank the rapid readings. The emergency crews get their scorecard. The results were 24-hour. The readings were rapid. The scorecard was rapid.

The reductions were emissions. The closeout was energy. The voucher were dynamics. The solar were voucher.
doe-osti-3376720-justification-that-the-: Am-241 got residue-justified, and this DOE text covers Thermo-Fisher defense. The pages detail the generated findings. The nuclear folks get their data. doe-osti-3409098-reliability-assessment-: Breakers got solid-state-assessed, and this DOE final covers circuit breaker reliability. The pages detail the assessment findings. govdocs-archive_org-ShatteringTheAbraham:
Shattering the Icon of Abraham Lincoln appeared as a reprint from the Journal of Historical Review, a journal known for revisionist takes on settled history. Its target is the honored public image of Lincoln, the president remembered as the Great Emancipator.

The piece argues against the standard story, drawing on claims about Freemasonry, the occult, and the politics around Lincoln's death. It belongs to a strain of writing that treats national heroes as masks for hidden forces. The library holds it as an archive item, presented without endorsement, so readers can judge the argument and its evidence for themselves.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RewaldRonaldRCI:
A news article reports the collapse of a Hawaii investment firm, Bishop, Baldwin, Rewald, Dillingham and Wong. Hundreds of investors lost their life savings in the firm. After the collapse, CIA lawyers moved to seal the firm's records. The agency's connection to the company became the story's center. The publication is not identified.

The Rewald case joined finance and intelligence in one scandal. A firm that sold investments also, its founder claimed, served the CIA. Sealed records kept the public from testing that claim in full. The article preserves the collapse as first reported: the losses, the lawyers, and the seal. It is a period account of a case where the paper trail itself was treated as a secret.
leonardo-da-vinci:
Maurice W. Brockwell wrote this short life of Leonardo da Vinci. Eight color reproductions illustrate the book, with the Mona Lisa as frontispiece. That painting hangs in the Louvre, the caption notes.

An English critic of 1721 praised Leonardo's happy genius, Brockwell quotes. He was consummate in art and knowing in the sciences, the critic said. Brockwell traces that many-sided career for general readers. Painting, invention, and court life all share his pages. The book serves as a compact doorway to Leonardo's world. Brockwell was a Leonardo scholar of long standing. Plates of paintings let readers test his judgments directly.
nasa-tm-19680004646-a-4500-deg-r-2500-de:
Jack G. Slaby, Byron L. Siegel, William F. Mattson, and William L. Maag, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, wrote this memorandum in January 1968. Numbered TM X-1506, it describes a flowing-gas facility that heats gas to forty-five hundred degrees Rankine. The facility let engineers test reactor fuel elements outside a reactor, at full working heat.

The heater stacks four identical stages, each run on its own, with flat tungsten plates as the heating elements. Tungsten plates were easy to heat electrically and easy to fabricate, and earlier tests ran them successfully at still higher surface temperatures. The finished heater raises hydrogen, helium, or nitrogen to the full outlet temperature. Sections cover power supply choice, feeding large currents while allowing expansion, matched materials, and operating goals. The report compares worked-out and measured surface temperature profiles, and a table lists operating conditions for each gas.
pastoral-poetry-pastoral-drama-a-literar: The hosted sample here shows only the front matter and contents of Pastoral Poetry and Pastoral Drama, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Walter W. Greg as the author and describes the book as a literary inquiry with special reference to the pre-Restoration stage in England. It was printed at Oxford in 1906. The contents promise chapters on foreign and English pastoral poetry, including Spenser and Milton's Lycidas, and on Italian pastoral drama.
peignot-dictionnaire-critique-litteraire: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the Google Books digital-copy notice pages that precede this scan, with no page of the work itself visible. The catalogue record names Gabriel Peignot as the author and dates the book 1806. Its full French title announces a critical, literary, and bibliographical dictionary of the principal books condemned to the fire, suppressed, or censored, preceded by a discourse on such works.
podcast-joerogan-XJGKdkQ25CI:
Thousands of JFK files released by the National Archives get covered in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. The document dump was required by law and long delayed. When it landed, researchers and the curious dove in at once, and Rogan followed the story.

The talk sorts what the release held: fresh pages, old pages with fewer black bars, and the files still held back. Rogan asks why a democracy needs sixty years to open its own records. The segment is a dated dispatch from a disclosure day, useful for anyone tracking how the Kennedy paper trail has grown.
podcast-joerogan-aV6VucHGrcI:
Philosopher Jack Symes joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2193 to talk about the good life. Symes hosts The Panpsycast, a philosophy podcast that brings academic thinkers to general listeners. Rogan gives him the long chair to ask what the great minds say about living well.

The two work through rival answers, from pleasure and virtue to meaning found in suffering. Symes keeps the tour clear and fair, giving each school its best case. Rogan tests the ideas against a fighter's and comic's life. The episode is philosophy as it should feel at a kitchen table: serious, plain, and aimed at Monday morning.
podcast-joerogan-lAYYmfoyLCI:
Aubrey Marcus sits with Rogan for episode 621 of the Joe Rogan Experience, an early talk on mind, body, and the examined life. Marcus had built Onnit, a fitness firm with a philosophy arm, and he was becoming a voice for optimization long before the word was everywhere.

The two talk training, purpose, and the habits Marcus credits for his drive, in the loose style of the young show. Rogan knows him as a friend and fellow seeker, and it shows. The episode is a fossil of the pre-optimization era, kept for listeners curious about where Marcus's later empire of self-work began.
tenting-to-night-a-chronicle-of-sport-an: Mary Roberts Rinehart wrote Tenting To-Night. Its subtitle calls it a record of sport and trips in Glacier Park. The Cascade Mountains share the ground. Houghton Mifflin issued the book in April 1918. Rights were held from 1917 by Cosmopolitan Magazine. Chapters listed start with The Trail and The Big Adventure. Bridge Creek to Bowman Lake comes next. A Fisherman's Paradise and To Kintla Lake follow. Running the Rapids of the Flathead closes the parts shown.
the-tragedies-of-the-medici: Edgcumbe Staley's Tragedies of the Medici, dedicated to his father's memory, is laid out here in a detailed contents list with no chapter text following. Six chapters promise the Pazzi conspiracy, the first tyrannicide, a father's vengeance among the Medici brothers, and three murdered princesses. Later headings cover Francesco and Bianca Cappello, and pathetic victims of fateful passion including Virginia de' Medici. Staley, author of The Guilds of Florence, arranged a family chronicle of poison, daggers, and doomed love, all of it outlined in these headings.
the-treasury-of-ancient-egypt-miscellane: Arthur E. P. B. Weigall, inspector-general of Upper Egypt for the Department of Antiquities, published The Treasury of Ancient Egypt with Rand McNally in 1912, subtitled miscellaneous chapters on ancient Egyptian history and archaeology. This record shows the frontispiece, showing Weigall beside the hawk-god Horus at Edfu, the title page, and a dedication to Alan H. Gardiner of Oxford recalling summer nights upon the Theban hills. The preface is headed but not given, and no chapter follows. Weigall's insider essays on pharaonic Egypt begin beyond the pages present.
